frictionVectors.title: EUROPEAN GAS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Europe relies on Algerian pipeline and LNG supplies, giving Algiers strategic leverage while exposing it to demands over pricing, migration, and regional alignment.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Sonatrach retains dominant control over oil and gas, but delayed diversification and subsidy pressures leave sovereignty vulnerable to energy-price swings and foreign technology needs.

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND DEBT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Angola retains formal ownership of hydrocarbons, but production declines, foreign operators, and debt-linked infrastructure financing constrain independent policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: LOBITO CORRIDOR CONTEST
frictionVectors.details: U.S., European, and Chinese interests are competing around the corridor's transport and critical-mineral potential, increasing Angola's leverage but also external pressure over infrastructure governance.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou is central to Benin's trade and revenue base, while foreign-funded modernization and regional transit relationships can limit autonomy over customs and infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL BORDER INSECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence near the Burkina Faso and Niger frontiers threatens transport corridors, agricultural zones, and state access to northern resources, drawing increased external security involvement.

frictionVectors.title: DIAMOND MARKET CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has secured stronger value-sharing arrangements with De Beers, but continued dependence on a concentrated global diamond market limits resilience and bargaining freedom.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL INFRASTRUCTURE GAP
frictionVectors.details: Copper, nickel, and battery-mineral prospects are attracting foreign capital, yet limited rail, power, and water infrastructure could shift value capture toward external investors.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SECTOR NATIONALIZATION
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking tighter state control over gold production and refining, but weak oversight, smuggling, and insecurity reduce the practical share of value retained by the state.

frictionVectors.title: SECURITY PARTNERSHIP DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from French cooperation toward Russian-linked security support has increased political autonomy rhetoric while creating new dependence on opaque external actors and military supply chains.

highlights: Mining nationalism meets weak bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state participation and processing value from nickel and rare-earth projects, but financing and technical dependence give foreign partners substantial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: GREAT LAKES BORDER PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and armed groups constrain trade routes and encourage reliance on external security and diplomatic partners.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND AIRSPACE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment and donor support remain important for ports, airports, and connectivity, creating long-term exposure to external commercial and strategic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY BURDEN
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing, narcotics trafficking, and search-and-rescue demands require cooperation with European and Atlantic partners, limiting fully autonomous maritime enforcement.

highlights: Oil and timber remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND MINING CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and lenders retain major influence across oil, gas, mining, and infrastructure, while weak transparency limits domestic capture of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE AND FAR NORTH CONFLICTS
frictionVectors.details: Insurgencies disrupt transport, agriculture, and local administration, while security dependence on external suppliers and partners increases pressure on state resources.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY-MINING NEXUS
frictionVectors.details: The government relies heavily on Russian-linked security support, while gold and diamond access remains opaque and difficult for state institutions to regulate.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR AND CUSTOMS FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Road insecurity and armed-group taxation along regional trade routes reduce public revenue and give neighboring states and private actors leverage over strategic supply lines.

frictionVectors.title: OIL REVENUE AND PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chad controls production politically but depends on foreign operators, export infrastructure, and transit through neighboring countries, leaving revenue and logistics externally vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: COMPETING SECURITY PARTNERS
frictionVectors.details: The government balances relationships with France, the United Arab Emirates, Sudan-linked networks, and other external actors as regional conflict increases demand for military and financial support.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and Maritime Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, keeping territorial sovereignty and migration management at the center of Comoros's foreign policy. Limited maritime enforcement capacity constrains control over surrounding waters.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on external donors and contractors for transport, energy, and port infrastructure. This dependence narrows government leverage over strategic assets and long-term development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: M23 Conflict and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Armed conflict in the east, linked to regional security competition and contested external support, continues to weaken Kinshasa's control over territory and mineral zones. Civilian displacement and informal taxation further undermine state authority.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and Copper Bargaining Power
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in copper and cobalt production, while the United States and Europe seek alternative access and supply-chain influence. The government is renegotiating for greater value capture, but processing and infrastructure gaps limit leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy and public finances remain highly exposed to offshore oil production and foreign energy operators. Price volatility and limited domestic refining capacity reduce sovereign control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese participation in roads, rail, and other infrastructure provides essential connectivity but can reinforce debt and procurement dependence. Brazzaville continues to balance these ties against Western financial oversight and energy interests.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire remains a global cocoa leader but captures a limited share of downstream processing and brand value. New sustainability and traceability rules from external markets could raise compliance costs for producers and exporters.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port, logistics, energy, and digital sectors are attracting French, Chinese, Gulf, and Turkish investment. Competition offers financing options but risks fragmented standards and continued foreign control of high-value infrastructure.

highlights: Ethiopian trade creates leverage and exposure

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military and Port Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through foreign military bases and competing port operators, giving the state revenue and diplomatic leverage while limiting independent control over strategic space. Rivalry among China, the United States, France, Japan, and other partners raises pressure on national alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Ethiopia Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's port economy is closely tied to Ethiopian trade and vulnerable to regional instability in the Red Sea and Horn of Africa. Large infrastructure financing obligations increase exposure to creditors and constrain fiscal autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Allocation
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to treat upstream Nile projects, especially Ethiopia's GERD, as a core national-security issue. Negotiations remain vulnerable to breakdown because Cairo seeks binding drought-management guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Gulf, IMF, and other external financing supports infrastructure and reserves but increases policy constraints. Strategic ports, energy assets, and state-linked projects remain exposed to foreign capital influence.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature fields and volatile production weaken the state's fiscal base. International oil companies and foreign technical capital retain substantial influence over remaining offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: Gas Monetization Constraints
frictionVectors.details: The country is pursuing gas processing and regional monetization, but limited domestic capacity and infrastructure make it dependent on external partners, shipping networks, and neighboring feedstock.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Power Competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline gives it strategic leverage amid competition involving Gulf states, Turkey, Egypt, and other external actors. Asmara seeks bargaining power while resisting formal dependence on any single sponsor.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining
frictionVectors.details: Mining provides hard currency but relies heavily on foreign operators, financing, and technical expertise. This creates tension between state revenue claims and concerns over transparency, labor, and environmental control.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Supply-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's fuel, trade, finance, and transport systems remain closely tied to South Africa and regional customs networks. This limits independent infrastructure and resource-security options.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and Agribusiness Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Sugar and related agriculture remain important revenue sources but are exposed to external market rules, water stress, and foreign buyers. Diversification efforts face limited capital and a small domestic market.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Strategic Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's control over domestic power generation and regional electricity ambitions. Egypt and Sudan continue to resist arrangements they view as insufficiently binding during prolonged drought.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-currency shortages, debt restructuring, and reliance on external corridors constrain Addis Ababa's strategic autonomy. Access to ports, telecom infrastructure, and major financing remains vulnerable to outside leverage.

highlights: Junta-led transition seeks tighter control over oil and manganese
French influence reduced, but external capital remains essential

frictionVectors.title: Resource renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pressing for greater state participation and local value addition in oil, manganese, and timber. Contract uncertainty could deter investment while increasing leverage for Gulf and Asian financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Transition legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: The military-led political transition has improved elite cohesion but leaves uncertainty over civilian rule, institutional checks, and the durability of new economic agreements.

highlights: Small-state sovereignty anchored by Senegalese security ties
Peanuts, fisheries, and port access remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for trade routes, electricity, security cooperation, and regional connectivity. This support stabilizes the country but narrows its independent strategic room.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and port pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and weak monitoring constrain sovereign control over marine resources. Banjul's port modernization and logistics ambitions remain dependent on external financing and operators.

highlights: Debt crisis drives renewed scrutiny of mining and energy concessions
Gold remains strategic, while illegal mining damages state control

frictionVectors.title: Gold and illegal mining
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal and illegal mining networks, including foreign-linked trading channels, erode fiscal capture and contaminate land and water. Efforts to formalize the sector face entrenched political and commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-for-resource leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal adjustment and restructuring have increased pressure to attract external capital into energy, minerals, and infrastructure. Ghana retains formal ownership, but financing needs constrain its bargaining power.

highlights: Bauxite powerhouse seeks downstream industrial control
Simandou promises transformation but deepens external dependence

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project depends on large foreign-led rail and port infrastructure, giving consortium partners substantial influence over logistics and export timing. The government is seeking local processing and stronger fiscal terms.

frictionVectors.title: Junta and mining governance
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities use resource nationalism to build legitimacy while relying on foreign mining companies and financiers. Political uncertainty and weak oversight raise risks of opaque contracts and uneven benefit sharing.

highlights: Cashew economy remains vulnerable to foreign traders and price shocks
Political instability limits control over ports, borders, and offshore assets

frictionVectors.title: Cashew dependency
frictionVectors.details: Most cashew production is exported with limited domestic processing, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to foreign buyers and volatile prices. India and other Asian markets remain especially influential in the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Institutional fragility and trafficking
frictionVectors.details: Recurring elite conflict and weak security institutions undermine oversight of ports, borders, fisheries, and offshore resources. Transnational trafficking networks exploit this governance gap and compete with formal state authority.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and large bilateral obligations constrain Nairobi's policy autonomy. Public resistance to taxation and austerity complicates efforts to restore sovereign control over infrastructure financing.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Port Corridor Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing Chinese-backed infrastructure, Gulf commercial interests, and regional competition over Mombasa and Lamu corridors. Security risks and uneven project economics limit bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but deepen structural dependence on Pretoria. Dam construction, compensation, and environmental impacts remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Labor Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's manufacturing base remains heavily dependent on external market access and foreign-owned factories. Any shift in trade preferences or investor sentiment could rapidly weaken domestic economic control.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Contract Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining concessions and rail-port arrangements give foreign operators substantial influence over Liberia's export infrastructure and fiscal revenues. The government is seeking better local value capture without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Shipping Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Liberia's maritime registry and major port assets attract foreign commercial interests while providing limited domestic industrial spillovers. Infrastructure financing and concession transparency remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security centers continue to contest control over oil facilities, budgets, and export flows. Foreign partnerships and parallel institutions weaken unified national command over strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Turkish and Russian Footprints
frictionVectors.details: Turkey's security and construction presence and Russia-linked military networks give external actors leverage over ports, bases, and political bargaining. This limits Libya's ability to convert energy wealth into autonomous state capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects remain dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented infrastructure. Revenue sharing, environmental damage, and community consent continue to challenge sovereign resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and limited transport capacity force Madagascar to rely on external investors for strategic infrastructure. This strengthens foreign bargaining power over mining expansion and export corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Fiscal Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking foreign capital for uranium, rare-earth and other mining projects while debt distress limits its bargaining leverage. Weak processing capacity risks leaving the country dependent on royalties rather than controlling value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower disruptions, fuel shortages and foreign-exchange scarcity constrain industrial sovereignty. Reliance on external lenders and imported energy leaves infrastructure planning vulnerable to donor and creditor priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Nationalism
frictionVectors.details: The military government is tightening state control over gold and renegotiating mining terms, but production still relies heavily on foreign operators, equipment and expertise. The resulting disputes risk litigation, investment delays and lower formal output.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mali's reliance on Russian-linked security support provides regime protection but increases exposure to opaque commercial and strategic arrangements. Persistent insurgency also threatens roads, mining zones and export corridors.

highlights: Gas Exporter at the Atlantic Frontier

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Project Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers Mauritania new export revenue and leverage, but dependence on foreign operators, offshore infrastructure and Senegalese coordination limits immediate sovereign control. Revenue transparency and local-content delivery remain central risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Corridor Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore remains concentrated around a foreign-linked rail and port system, leaving the state exposed to commodity cycles and infrastructure bottlenecks. Plans to diversify minerals and logistics could improve leverage if domestic processing advances.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Maritime Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos settlement and future administration of Diego Garcia remain strategically sensitive because of the base's military importance and wider Indian Ocean competition. Mauritius must balance sovereignty claims with security, diplomatic and economic realities.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital in Critical Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese, Gulf and Western interests compete for influence in ports, digital networks and logistics. Mauritius retains strong institutions, but its small market and import dependence constrain autonomy during major-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is expanding infrastructure, renewables and phosphate-linked activity in Western Sahara, strengthening its practical control while facing continuing legal and diplomatic challenges over resource consent and territorial status.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Partners in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf and Chinese capital supports ports, rail, renewable energy and electric-vehicle supply chains. These partnerships increase industrial capacity but create exposure to external financing conditions and geopolitical competition.

highlights: LNG Ambitions Meet Cabo Delgado Insecurity

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency continues to constrain the state's control over gas-rich northern territory and has left major LNG projects reliant on foreign security support. Any sustained offensive could delay production and deepen external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Revenue and Sovereign Debt
frictionVectors.details: Future gas revenues remain central to fiscal recovery, but financing obligations and international project operators limit Maputo's near-term bargaining power over the sector.

highlights: Oil and Green Hydrogen Raise Bargaining Power

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Emerging Energy Assets
frictionVectors.details: International firms dominate capital and technical capacity in offshore oil and green-hydrogen projects, creating a risk that Namibia captures less value than expected without stronger local-content and fiscal terms.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, logistics, and port infrastructure attract competing Chinese, Western, and regional interests. Windhoek is using diversification to preserve strategic room, but infrastructure financing remains externally exposed.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Contract Tensions
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are pressing for greater control and revenue from uranium and other minerals while relations with former Western partners deteriorate. Contract disputes and diplomatic isolation could reduce technical capacity and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export Corridor Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Niger's access to export infrastructure depends heavily on cross-border routes and regional political relations. Insecurity and strained ties with coastal neighbors threaten the reliability of its oil logistics.

highlights: Reform Seeks Control of a Leaking Oil State
Gas and Critical Infrastructure Face Security Risk

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Oil-Sector Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International operators remain important to upstream investment, technology, and financing, while production-sharing arrangements and weak regulation limit the state's effective control over value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Regional Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and violence in the Niger Delta and northern corridors continue to undermine energy revenues and infrastructure reliability. These pressures increase dependence on private security and external technical support.

highlights: Mineral Value Chains Remain Externally Linked

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral and Security Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo generate intense diplomatic pressure and sanctions risk. The dispute directly threatens Kigali's access to trade, finance, and strategic partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Aid, Technology, and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control but relies on external donors, investors, and technology providers for infrastructure and development finance. Geopolitical scrutiny is narrowing the room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: Uncertain hydrocarbon prospects limit immediate fiscal gains, while licensing decisions could increase dependence on external energy firms. Maritime boundary and Gulf of Guinea security concerns remain persistent.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, and energy upgrades rely heavily on foreign finance and contractors, narrowing São Tomé and Príncipe's room to negotiate on strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND GAS GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Emerging offshore production can strengthen state revenues, but contract transparency, local-content delivery, and revenue management will determine whether resource control improves.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND FOREIGN ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing access and depleted stocks generate domestic pressure against foreign fleets, especially where licensing revenue conflicts with coastal livelihoods and food security.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from external naval and coast-guard cooperation in the western Indian Ocean, but balancing Indian, European, Chinese, and other interests is strategically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, ports, energy, and climate-resilience projects depend on foreign capital and concessional finance, leaving the country vulnerable to external financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACTS AND VALUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects can expand export earnings, but foreign ownership, tax terms, environmental impacts, and limited local processing constrain sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Mining logistics and transport infrastructure are closely tied to external investors and commodity demand, creating vulnerability to contract disputes and price swings.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND SECURITY SPONSORS
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other partners shape port, security, and infrastructure outcomes, while competing external relationships can limit unified Somali control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE GOVERNANCE FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Disputes between the federal government and member states over hydrocarbons, fisheries, and licensing weaken national bargaining power and create openings for foreign firms and political patrons.

highlights: Grid and freight bottlenecks constrain sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL VALUE-CHAIN PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for preferential access to South Africa's platinum-group metals, manganese, and other strategic minerals. Pretoria is seeking local beneficiation while remaining dependent on external capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: LOGISTICS AND ENERGY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, rail constraints, and port congestion weaken the state's ability to monetize its resource base. Private operators and foreign-linked suppliers are gaining influence as public infrastructure capacity erodes.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the state lifeline

frictionVectors.title: OIL-EXPORT VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's fiscal survival depends on oil routed through Sudan, leaving revenue and exports exposed to Sudan's war, pipeline disruption, and opaque fee arrangements. External firms and neighboring states retain substantial leverage over production and transit.

frictionVectors.title: REGIONAL SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Implementation of the peace process remains dependent on regional diplomacy, donor funding, and externally supported security arrangements. Internal elite competition and subnational violence continue to limit effective sovereign control.

highlights: Red Sea access becomes strategic prize

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trade are central to financing rival armed networks, with regional intermediaries and external buyers benefiting from weak oversight. Control of mines, transport corridors, and export channels remains contested.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND SUPPLY-CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Sudan's Red Sea coastline and Port Sudan are increasingly important to competing regional powers seeking maritime access and logistical influence. Damage to infrastructure and rival control of corridors undermine national ownership of strategic assets.

highlights: Gas and minerals drive bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: LNG NEGOTIATION LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is using its offshore gas reserves and planned LNG development to attract investment while pressing for stronger domestic benefits. Foreign capital, technology, and offtake arrangements could still limit local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL GEOPOLITICS
frictionVectors.details: The Dar es Salaam corridor is attracting competing Chinese, Gulf, Western, and regional infrastructure interests. Expanded connectivity improves national leverage but creates exposure to external control over logistics and strategic mineral flows.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRANSIT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's port and hinterland trade generate strategic revenue, but the system depends on foreign shipping, finance, and neighboring-country demand. External investors retain meaningful influence over logistics infrastructure and customs-linked value chains.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SPILLOVER RISK
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and illicit trafficking pressure northern Togo and threaten transport routes linking the coast to Burkina Faso and Niger. Security partnerships and imported surveillance and defense capabilities are becoming increasingly important to protecting sovereign corridors.

frictionVectors.title: EU MIGRATION AND FINANCIAL LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: European funding and migration cooperation give the EU substantial influence over Tunisia's policy space. Disputes over implementation, human rights, and fiscal conditions remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY IMPORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic production and reliance on imported hydrocarbons constrain Tunisia's strategic autonomy. Renewable investment is growing, but financing and grid limitations slow substitution.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP AND OIL SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline ties Uganda's oil future to foreign investors, Tanzanian transit infrastructure, and Chinese financing. Environmental opposition and external pressure increase political and reputational costs.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT AND STRATEGIC INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure commitments have increased exposure to external creditors and contractors. Kampala is balancing Chinese capital with Gulf, Western, and regional partnerships to preserve room for maneuver.

highlights: Debt restructuring restores room to maneuver

frictionVectors.title: COPPER OWNERSHIP AND VALUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater fiscal returns, local processing, and transparency from multinational mining investors. Competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked firms creates leverage but also risks renewed dependency.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND EXPORT CORRIDOR BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and weak transport links limit copper expansion and industrial sovereignty. The Lobito Corridor offers diversification from traditional routes, but requires sustained external financing and regional coordination.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using export restrictions and beneficiation demands to capture more value from lithium, platinum, and other minerals. Foreign capital remains indispensable, leaving enforcement and ownership arrangements vulnerable to opaque bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: SANCTIONS, DEBT, AND CURRENCY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, arrears, and limited access to concessional finance constrain infrastructure investment and monetary sovereignty. Reliance on foreign currency and informal financing channels further weakens state control over the resource economy.
